views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:
Weak convergence of finite measures implies that the limsup of the measures of any closed set is
at most the measure of the closed set under the limit measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.FiniteMeasure.limsup_measure_closed_le_of_tendsto {Ω ι : Type*} {L : Filter ι} [MeasurableSpace Ω] [TopologicalSpace Ω] [HasOuterApproxClosed Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω] {μ : FiniteMeasure Ω} {μs : ι → FiniteMeasure Ω} (μs_lim : Tendsto μs L (𝓝 μ)) {F : Set Ω} (F_closed : IsClosed F) : (L.limsup fun i ↦ (μs i : Measure Ω) F) ≤ (μ : Measure Ω) F

views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:
Weak convergence of probability measures implies that the limsup of the measures of any closed
set is at most the measure of the closed set under the limit probability measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.limsup_measure_closed_le_of_tendsto {Ω ι : Type*} {L : Filter ι} [MeasurableSpace Ω] [TopologicalSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω] [HasOuterApproxClosed Ω] {μ : ProbabilityMeasure Ω} {μs : ι → ProbabilityMeasure Ω} (μs_lim : Tendsto μs L (𝓝 μ)) {F : Set Ω} (F_closed : IsClosed F) : (L.limsup fun i ↦ (μs i : Measure Ω) F) ≤ (μ : Measure Ω) F

views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:
Weak convergence of probability measures implies that the liminf of the measures of any open set
is at least the measure of the open set under the limit probability measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.le_liminf_measure_open_of_tendsto {Ω ι : Type*} {L : Filter ι} [MeasurableSpace Ω] [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω] [HasOuterApproxClosed Ω] {μ : ProbabilityMeasure Ω} {μs : ι → ProbabilityMeasure Ω} (μs_lim : Tendsto μs L (𝓝 μ)) {G : Set Ω} (G_open : IsOpen G) : (μ : Measure Ω) G ≤ L.liminf fun i ↦ (μs i : Measure Ω) G

views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:
Weak convergence of probability measures implies that if the boundary of a Borel set
carries no probability mass under the limit measure, then the limit of the measures of the set
equals the measure of the set under the limit probability measure.

A version with coercions to ordinary `ℝ≥0∞`-valued measures is
`MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_measure_of_null_frontier_of_tendsto'`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_measure_of_null_frontier_of_tendsto {Ω ι : Type*} {L : Filter ι} [MeasurableSpace Ω] [PseudoEMetricSpace Ω] [OpensMeasurableSpace Ω] [HasOuterApproxClosed Ω] {μ : ProbabilityMeasure Ω} {μs : ι → ProbabilityMeasure Ω} (μs_lim : Tendsto μs L (𝓝 μ)) {E : Set Ω} (E_nullbdry : μ (frontier E) = 0) : Tendsto (fun i ↦ μs i E) L (𝓝 (μ E))

views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:

candidate limit probability measure μ we have convergence of the measures μsᵢ(E) to μ(E),
then for all closed sets F we have the limsup condition limsup μsᵢ(F) ≤ μ(F).

views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:
Assuming that for all Borel sets E whose boundary ∂E carries no probability mass under a
candidate limit probability measure μ we have convergence of the measures μsᵢ(E) to μ(E),
then for all open sets G we have the limsup condition μ(G) ≤ liminf μsᵢ(G).

views.nl_informal:
One implication of the portmanteau theorem:
If for all open sets G we have the liminf condition `μ(G) ≤ liminf μsₙ(G)`, then the measures
μsₙ converge weakly to the measure μ.

views.nl_informal:
Continuity from below: the measure of the union of a sequence of (not necessarily measurable)
sets is the limit of the measures of the partial unions.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.tendsto_measure_iUnion_accumulate {ι : Type*} [Preorder ι] [IsCountablyGenerated (atTop : Filter ι)] {μ : ProbabilityMeasure Ω} {f : ι → Set Ω} : Tendsto (fun i ↦ μ (Accumulate f i)) atTop (𝓝 (μ (⋃ i, f i)))

views.nl_informal:
The monoidal product is a measurable function from the product of probability spaces over
`α` and `β` into the type of probability spaces over `α × β`. Lemma 4.1 of [A synthetic approach to
Markov kernels, conditional independence and theorems on sufficient statistics][fritz2020].

views.nl_informal:
A characterization of weak convergence of probability measures by the condition that the
integrals of every continuous bounded nonnegative function converge to the integral of the function
against the limit measure.

The characterization of weak convergence of probability measures by the usual (defining)
condition that the integrals of every continuous bounded function converge to the integral of the
function against the limit measure.

views.nl_informal:
Averaging with respect to a finite measure is the same as integrating against
`MeasureTheory.FiniteMeasure.normalize`.

If the normalized versions of finite measures converge weakly and their total masses
also converge, then the finite measures themselves converge weakly.

If finite measures themselves converge weakly to a nonzero limit measure, then their
normalized versions also converge weakly.

The weak convergence of finite measures to a nonzero limit can be characterized by the weak
convergence of both their normalized versions (probability measures) and their total masses.

views.nl_informal:
If `f : X → Y` is continuous and `Y` is equipped with the Borel sigma algebra, then
convergence (in distribution) of `ProbabilityMeasure`s on `X` implies convergence (in
distribution) of the push-forwards of these measures by `f`.

If `f : X → Y` is continuous and `Y` is equipped with the Borel sigma algebra, then
the push-forward of probability measures `f* : ProbabilityMeasure X → ProbabilityMeasure Y`
is continuous (in the topologies of convergence in distribution).
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.ProbabilityMeasure.continuous_map {f : Ω → Ω'} (f_cont : Continuous f) : Continuous (fun ν ↦ ProbabilityMeasure.map ν f_cont.measurable.aemeasurable)

views.nl_informal:
If `ν` is a finite measure, and `s ⊆ α × β` is measurable, then `x ↦ ν { y | (x, y) ∈ s }` is
a measurable function. `measurable_measure_prodMk_left` is strictly more general.
views.lean_signature: theorem measurable_measure_prodMk_left_finite [IsFiniteMeasure ν] {s : Set (α × β)} (hs : MeasurableSet s) : Measurable fun x => ν (Prod.mk x ⁻¹' s)

views.nl_informal:
If `ν` is an s-finite measure, and `s ⊆ α × β` is measurable, then `x ↦ ν { y | (x, y) ∈ s }`
is a measurable function.

Not true without the s-finite assumption: on `ℝ × ℝ` with the product sigma-algebra, let `s` be the
diagonal and let `ν` be an uncountable sum of Dirac measures (all Dirac measures for points in a
set `t`). Then `ν (Prod.mk x ⁻¹' s) = ν {x} = if x ∈ t then 1 else 0`. If `t` is chosen
non-measurable, this will not be measurable.
views.lean_signature: theorem measurable_measure_prodMk_left [SFinite ν] {s : Set (α × β)} (hs : MeasurableSet s) : Measurable fun x => ν (Prod.mk x ⁻¹' s)

views.nl_informal:
If `μ` is an s-finite measure, and `s ⊆ α × β` is measurable, then `y ↦ μ { x | (x, y) ∈ s }` is
a measurable function.
views.lean_signature: theorem measurable_measure_prodMk_right {μ : Measure α} [SFinite μ] {s : Set (α × β)} (hs : MeasurableSet s) : Measurable fun y => μ ((fun x => (x, y)) ⁻¹' s)

The Lebesgue integral is measurable. This shows that the integrand of (the right-hand-side of)
Tonelli's theorem is measurable.

The Lebesgue integral is measurable. This shows that the integrand of (the right-hand-side of)
Tonelli's theorem is measurable.

views.nl_informal:
The Lebesgue integral is measurable. This shows that the integrand of (the right-hand-side of)
the symmetric version of Tonelli's theorem is measurable.
views.lean_signature: theorem Measurable.lintegral_prod_left' [SFinite μ] {f : α × β → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable f) : Measurable fun y => ∫⁻ x, f (x, y) ∂μ

views.nl_informal:
The Lebesgue integral is measurable. This shows that the integrand of (the right-hand-side of)
the symmetric version of Tonelli's theorem is measurable.
This version has the argument `f` in curried form.
views.lean_signature: theorem Measurable.lintegral_prod_left [SFinite μ] {f : α → β → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable (uncurry f)) : Measurable fun y => ∫⁻ x, f x y ∂μ

views.nl_informal:
For any measures `μ` and `ν` and any sets `s` and `t`,
we have `μ.prod ν (s ×ˢ t) ≤ μ s * ν t`.

If `ν` is an s-finite measure (which is usually true),
then this inequality becomes an equality, see `prod_prod` below.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.prod_prod_le (s : Set α) (t : Set β) : μ.prod ν (s ×ˢ t) ≤ μ s * ν t

views.nl_informal:
The product measure of the product of two sets is the product of their measures. Note that we
do not need the sets to be measurable.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.prod_prod (s : Set α) (t : Set β) : μ.prod ν (s ×ˢ t) = μ s * ν t

views.nl_informal:
If `μ`-a.e. section `{y | (x, y) ∈ s}` of a measurable set have `ν` measure zero,
then `s` has `μ.prod ν` measure zero.

This implication requires `s` to be measurable but does not require `ν` to be s-finite.
See also `measure_prod_null` and `measure_ae_null_of_prod_null` below.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.measure_prod_null_of_ae_null {s : Set (α × β)} (hsm : MeasurableSet s) (hs : (fun x => ν (Prod.mk x ⁻¹' s)) =ᵐ[μ] 0) : μ.prod ν s = 0

views.nl_informal:
A measurable set `s` has `μ.prod ν` measure zero, where `ν` is an s-finite measure,
if and only if `μ`-a.e. section `{y | (x, y) ∈ s}` of `s` have `ν` measure zero.

See `measure_ae_null_of_prod_null` for the forward implication without the measurability assumption
and `measure_prod_null_of_ae_null` for the reverse implication without the s-finiteness assumption.

Note: the assumption `hs` cannot be dropped. For a counterexample, see
Walter Rudin *Real and Complex Analysis*, example (c) in section 8.9.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.measure_prod_null {s : Set (α × β)} (hs : MeasurableSet s) : μ.prod ν s = 0 ↔ (fun x => ν (Prod.mk x ⁻¹' s)) =ᵐ[μ] 0

views.nl_informal: If `s ×ˢ t` is a null measurable set and `μ s ≠ 0`, then `t` is a null measurable set.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.right_of_prod {s : Set α} {t : Set β} (h : NullMeasurableSet (s ×ˢ t) (μ.prod ν)) (hs : μ s ≠ 0) : NullMeasurableSet t ν

views.nl_informal: If `Prod.snd ⁻¹' t` is a null measurable set and `μ ≠ 0`, then `t` is a null measurable set.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.of_preimage_snd [NeZero μ] {t : Set β} (h : NullMeasurableSet (Prod.snd ⁻¹' t) (μ.prod ν)) : NullMeasurableSet t ν

views.nl_informal:
`Prod.snd ⁻¹' t` is null measurable w.r.t. `μ.prod ν` iff `t` is null measurable w.r.t. `ν`
provided that `μ ≠ 0`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.nullMeasurableSet_preimage_snd [NeZero μ] {t : Set β} : NullMeasurableSet (Prod.snd ⁻¹' t) (μ.prod ν) ↔ NullMeasurableSet t ν

views.nl_informal:
A measure on a product space equals the product measure if they are equal on rectangles
with as sides sets that generate the corresponding σ-algebras.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.prod_eq_generateFrom {μ : Measure α} {ν : Measure β} {C : Set (Set α)} {D : Set (Set β)} (hC : generateFrom C = ‹_›) (hD : generateFrom D = ‹_›) (h2C : IsPiSystem C) (h2D : IsPiSystem D) (h3C : μ.FiniteSpanningSetsIn C) (h3D : ν.FiniteSpanningSetsIn D) {μν : Measure (α × β)} (h₁ : ∀ s ∈ C, ∀ t ∈ D, μν (s ×ˢ t) = μ s * ν t) : μ.prod ν = μν

views.nl_informal:
A measure on a product space equals the product measure of sigma-finite measures if they are
equal on rectangles.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.prod_eq {μ : Measure α} [SigmaFinite μ] {ν : Measure β} [SigmaFinite ν] {μν : Measure (α × β)} (h : ∀ s t, MeasurableSet s → MeasurableSet t → μν (s ×ˢ t) = μ s * ν t) : μ.prod ν = μν

views.nl_informal: If `s ×ˢ t` is a null measurable set and `ν t ≠ 0`, then `s` is a null measurable set.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.left_of_prod {s : Set α} {t : Set β} (h : NullMeasurableSet (s ×ˢ t) (μ.prod ν)) (ht : ν t ≠ 0) : NullMeasurableSet s μ

views.nl_informal: If `Prod.fst ⁻¹' s` is a null measurable set and `ν ≠ 0`, then `s` is a null measurable set.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.NullMeasurableSet.of_preimage_fst [NeZero ν] {s : Set α} (h : NullMeasurableSet (Prod.fst ⁻¹' s) (μ.prod ν)) : NullMeasurableSet s μ

views.nl_informal:
`Prod.fst ⁻¹' s` is null measurable w.r.t. `μ.prod ν` iff `s` is null measurable w.r.t. `μ`
provided that `ν ≠ 0`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.nullMeasurableSet_preimage_fst [NeZero ν] {s : Set α} : NullMeasurableSet (Prod.fst ⁻¹' s) (μ.prod ν) ↔ NullMeasurableSet s μ

views.nl_informal:
The product of two non-null sets is null measurable
if and only if both of them are null measurable.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.nullMeasurableSet_prod_of_ne_zero {s : Set α} {t : Set β} (hs : μ s ≠ 0) (ht : ν t ≠ 0) : NullMeasurableSet (s ×ˢ t) (μ.prod ν) ↔ NullMeasurableSet s μ ∧ NullMeasurableSet t ν

The product of two sets is null measurable
if and only if both of them are null measurable or one of them has measure zero.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.nullMeasurableSet_prod {s : Set α} {t : Set β} : NullMeasurableSet (s ×ˢ t) (μ.prod ν) ↔ NullMeasurableSet s μ ∧ NullMeasurableSet t ν ∨ μ s = 0 ∨ ν t = 0

views.nl_informal:
Let `f : α → β` be a measure preserving map.
For a.e. all `a`, let `g a : γ → δ` be a measure preserving map.
Also suppose that `g` is measurable as a function of two arguments.
Then the map `fun (a, c) ↦ (f a, g a c)` is a measure preserving map
for the product measures on `α × γ` and `β × δ`.

Some authors call a map of the form `fun (a, c) ↦ (f a, g a c)` a *skew product* over `f`,
thus the choice of a name.

the integral of `f` is equal to the iterated integral.

views.nl_informal:
**Tonelli's Theorem**: For `ℝ≥0∞`-valued measurable functions on `α × β`,
the integral of `f` is equal to the iterated integral.

and `t` respectively.

This lemma shows that `restrict` and `toOuterMeasure` commute. Note that the LHS has a
restrict on measures and the RHS has a restrict on outer measures.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_toOuterMeasure_eq_toOuterMeasure_restrict (h : MeasurableSet s) : (μ.restrict s).toOuterMeasure = OuterMeasure.restrict s μ.toOuterMeasure

views.nl_informal:
If `t` is a measurable set, then the measure of `t` with respect to the restriction of
the measure to `s` equals the outer measure of `t ∩ s`. An alternate version requiring that `s`
be measurable instead of `t` exists as `Measure.restrict_apply'`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_apply (ht : MeasurableSet t) : μ.restrict s t = μ (t ∩ s)

views.nl_informal: Restriction of a measure to a subset is monotone both in set and in measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_mono' {_m0 : MeasurableSpace α} ⦃s s' : Set α⦄ ⦃μ ν : Measure α⦄ (hs : s ≤ᵐ[μ] s') (hμν : μ ≤ ν) : μ.restrict s ≤ ν.restrict s'

views.nl_informal: Restriction of a measure to a subset is monotone both in set and in measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_mono {_m0 : MeasurableSpace α} ⦃s s' : Set α⦄ (hs : s ⊆ s') ⦃μ ν : Measure α⦄ (hμν : μ ≤ ν) : μ.restrict s ≤ ν.restrict s'

views.nl_informal:
If `s` is a measurable set, then the outer measure of `t` with respect to the restriction of
the measure to `s` equals the outer measure of `t ∩ s`. This is an alternate version of
`Measure.restrict_apply`, requiring that `s` is measurable instead of `t`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_apply' (hs : MeasurableSet s) : μ.restrict s t = μ (t ∩ s)

views.nl_informal:
The restriction of the pushforward measure is the pushforward of the restriction. For a version
assuming only `AEMeasurable`, see `restrict_map_of_aemeasurable`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_map {f : α → β} (hf : Measurable f) {s : Set β} (hs : MeasurableSet s) : (μ.map f).restrict s = (μ.restrict <| f ⁻¹' s).map f

views.nl_informal:
If two measures agree on all measurable subsets of `s` and `t`, then they agree on all
measurable subsets of `s ∪ t`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_union_congr : μ.restrict (s ∪ t) = ν.restrict (s ∪ t) ↔ μ.restrict s = ν.restrict s ∧ μ.restrict t = ν.restrict t

views.nl_informal: This lemma shows that `Inf` and `restrict` commute for measures.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.restrict_sInf_eq_sInf_restrict {m0 : MeasurableSpace α} {m : Set (Measure α)} (hm : m.Nonempty) (ht : MeasurableSet t) : (sInf m).restrict t = sInf ((fun μ : Measure α => μ.restrict t) '' m)

views.nl_informal:
If a quasi measure preserving map `f` maps a set `s` to a set `t`,
then it is quasi measure preserving with respect to the restrictions of the measures.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.QuasiMeasurePreserving.restrict {ν : Measure β} {f : α → β} (hf : QuasiMeasurePreserving f μ ν) {t : Set β} (hmaps : MapsTo f s t) : QuasiMeasurePreserving f (μ.restrict s) (ν.restrict t)

views.nl_informal:
Two measures are equal if they have equal restrictions on a spanning collection of sets
(formulated using `Union`).
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_iff_of_iUnion_eq_univ [Countable ι] {s : ι → Set α} (hs : ⋃ i, s i = univ) : μ = ν ↔ ∀ i, μ.restrict (s i) = ν.restrict (s i)

views.nl_informal:
Two measures are equal if they have equal restrictions on a spanning collection of sets
(formulated using `biUnion`).
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_iff_of_biUnion_eq_univ {S : Set ι} {s : ι → Set α} (hc : S.Countable) (hs : ⋃ i ∈ S, s i = univ) : μ = ν ↔ ∀ i ∈ S, μ.restrict (s i) = ν.restrict (s i)

views.nl_informal:
Two measures are equal if they have equal restrictions on a spanning collection of sets
(formulated using `sUnion`).
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.ext_iff_of_sUnion_eq_univ {S : Set (Set α)} (hc : S.Countable) (hs : ⋃₀ S = univ) : μ = ν ↔ ∀ s ∈ S, μ.restrict s = ν.restrict s

views.nl_informal:
Two measures are equal if they are equal on the π-system generating the σ-algebra,
and they are both finite on an increasing spanning sequence of sets in the π-system.
This lemma is formulated using `sUnion`.

views.nl_informal:
Two measures are equal if they are equal on the π-system generating the σ-algebra,
and they are both finite on an increasing spanning sequence of sets in the π-system.

views.nl_informal:
If two measurable sets are ae_eq then any proposition that is almost everywhere true on one
is almost everywhere true on the other

views.nl_informal:
If two measurable sets are ae_eq then any proposition that is almost everywhere true on one
is almost everywhere true on the other
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.ae_restrict_congr_set {s t} (hst : s =ᵐ[μ] t) {p : α → Prop} : (∀ᵐ x ∂μ.restrict s, p x) ↔ ∀ᵐ x ∂μ.restrict t, p x

views.nl_informal: The set of measurable sets is measure-dense.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.measureDense_measurableSet : μ.MeasureDense {s | MeasurableSet s}

views.nl_informal:
If a family of sets `𝒜` is measure-dense in `X`, then any measurable set with finite measure
can be approximated by sets in `𝒜` with finite measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.MeasureDense.fin_meas_approx (h𝒜 : μ.MeasureDense 𝒜) {s : Set X} (ms : MeasurableSet s) (hμs : μ s ≠ ∞) (ε : ℝ) (ε_pos : 0 < ε) : ∃ t ∈ 𝒜, μ t ≠ ∞ ∧ μ (s ∆ t) < ENNReal.ofReal ε

views.nl_informal:
If `𝒜` is a measure-dense family of sets and `c : E`, then the set of constant indicators
with constant `c` whose underlying set is in `𝒜` is dense in the set of constant indicators
which are in `Lp E p μ` when `1 ≤ p < ∞`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.MeasureDense.indicatorConstLp_subset_closure (h𝒜 : μ.MeasureDense 𝒜) (c : E) : {indicatorConstLp p hs hμs c | (s : Set X) (hs : MeasurableSet s) (hμs : μ s ≠ ∞)} ⊆ closure {indicatorConstLp p (h𝒜.measurable s hs) hμs c | (s : Set X) (hs : s ∈ 𝒜) (hμs : μ s ≠ ∞)}

views.nl_informal:
If a family of sets `𝒜` is measure-dense in `X`, then it is also the case for the sets in `𝒜`
with finite measure.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.MeasureDense.fin_meas (h𝒜 : μ.MeasureDense 𝒜) : μ.MeasureDense {s | s ∈ 𝒜 ∧ μ s ≠ ∞}

views.nl_informal:
If a measurable space equipped with a finite measure is generated by an algebra of sets, then
this algebra of sets is measure-dense.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.MeasureDense.of_generateFrom_isSetAlgebra_finite [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h𝒜 : IsSetAlgebra 𝒜) (hgen : m = MeasurableSpace.generateFrom 𝒜) : μ.MeasureDense 𝒜

views.nl_informal:
If a measure space `X` is generated by an algebra of sets which contains a monotone countable
family of sets with finite measure spanning `X` (thus the measure is `σ`-finite), then this algebra
of sets is measure-dense.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.MeasureDense.of_generateFrom_isSetAlgebra_sigmaFinite (h𝒜 : IsSetAlgebra 𝒜) (S : μ.FiniteSpanningSetsIn 𝒜) (hgen : m = MeasurableSpace.generateFrom 𝒜) : μ.MeasureDense 𝒜

views.nl_informal: By definition, a separable measure admits a countable and measure-dense family of sets.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.exists_countable_measureDense [IsSeparable μ] : ∃ 𝒜, 𝒜.Countable ∧ μ.MeasureDense 𝒜

views.nl_informal:
If a measurable space is countably generated and equipped with a `σ`-finite measure, then the
measure is separable. This is not an instance because it is used below to prove the more
general case where `μ` is s-finite.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isSeparable_of_sigmaFinite [CountablyGenerated X] [SigmaFinite μ] : IsSeparable μ

views.nl_informal:
If a compact interval `[a, b]` is covered by a union of open interval `(c i, d i)`, then
`f b - f a ≤ ∑ f (d i) - f (c i)`. This is an auxiliary technical statement to prove the same
statement for half-open intervals, the point of the current statement being that one can use
compactness to reduce it to a finite sum, and argue by induction on the size of the covering set.
views.lean_signature: theorem StieltjesFunction.length_subadditive_Icc_Ioo {a b : ℝ} {c d : ℕ → ℝ} (ss : Icc a b ⊆ ⋃ i, Ioo (c i) (d i)) : ofReal (f b - f a) ≤ ∑' i, ofReal (f (d i) - f (c i))

views.nl_informal:
A set of measures `S` is tight if for all `0 < ε`, there exists a compact set `K` such that
for all `μ ∈ S`, `μ Kᶜ ≤ ε`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.IsTightMeasureSet_iff_exists_isCompact_measure_compl_le : IsTightMeasureSet S ↔ ∀ ε, 0 < ε → ∃ K : Set 𝓧, IsCompact K ∧ ∀ μ ∈ S, μ (Kᶜ) ≤ ε

views.nl_informal: Finite measures that are inner regular with respect to closed compact sets are tight.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isTightMeasureSet_singleton_of_innerRegularWRT [OpensMeasurableSpace 𝓧] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] (h : μ.InnerRegularWRT (fun s ↦ IsCompact s ∧ IsClosed s) MeasurableSet) : IsTightMeasureSet {μ}

views.nl_informal: Inner regular finite measures on T2 spaces are tight.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isTightMeasureSet_singleton_of_innerRegular [T2Space 𝓧] [OpensMeasurableSpace 𝓧] [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [h : μ.InnerRegular] : IsTightMeasureSet {μ}

views.nl_informal: In a complete second-countable pseudo-metric space, finite measures are tight.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isTightMeasureSet_singleton {α : Type*} {mα : MeasurableSpace α} [PseudoEMetricSpace α] [CompleteSpace α] [SecondCountableTopology α] [BorelSpace α] {μ : Measure α} [IsFiniteMeasure μ] : IsTightMeasureSet {μ}

views.nl_informal: In a compact space, every set of measures is tight.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.IsTightMeasureSet.of_compactSpace [CompactSpace 𝓧] : IsTightMeasureSet S

views.nl_informal:
In a proper pseudo-metric space, a set of measures `S` is tight if and only if
the function `r ↦ ⨆ μ ∈ S, μ (Metric.closedBall x r)ᶜ` tends to `0` at infinity.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isTightMeasureSet_iff_tendsto_measure_compl_closedBall [ProperSpace E] (x : E) : IsTightMeasureSet S ↔ Tendsto (fun r : ℝ ↦ ⨆ μ ∈ S, μ (Metric.closedBall x r)ᶜ) atTop (𝓝 0)

views.nl_informal:
In a proper normed group, a set of measures `S` is tight if and only if
the function `r ↦ ⨆ μ ∈ S, μ {x | r < ‖x‖}` tends to `0` at infinity.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isTightMeasureSet_iff_tendsto_measure_norm_gt [ProperSpace E] : IsTightMeasureSet S ↔ Tendsto (fun r : ℝ ↦ ⨆ μ ∈ S, μ {x | r < ‖x‖}) atTop (𝓝 0)

views.nl_informal:
In a finite-dimensional inner product space,
a set of measures `S` is tight if and only if the function `r ↦ ⨆ μ ∈ S, μ {x | r < |⟪y, x⟫|}`
tends to `0` at infinity for all `y`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.isTightMeasureSet_iff_inner_tendsto : IsTightMeasureSet S ↔ ∀ y, Tendsto (fun r : ℝ ↦ ⨆ μ ∈ S, μ {x | r < ‖⟪y, x⟫_𝕜‖}) atTop (𝓝 0)

views.nl_informal:
This is Exercise 1.2.1 from [tao2010]. It allows you to express integration of a measurable
function with respect to `(μ.withDensity f)` as an integral with respect to `μ`, called the base
measure. `μ` is often the Lebesgue measure, and in this circumstance `f` is the probability density
function, and `(μ.withDensity f)` represents any continuous random variable as a
probability measure, such as the uniform distribution between 0 and 1, the Gaussian distribution,
the exponential distribution, the Beta distribution, or the Cauchy distribution (see Section 2.4
of [wasserman2004]). Thus, this method shows how to one can calculate expectations, variances,
and other moments as a function of the probability density function.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.lintegral_withDensity_eq_lintegral_mul (μ : Measure α) {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (h_mf : Measurable f) : ∀ {g : α → ℝ≥0∞}, Measurable g → ∫⁻ a, g a ∂μ.withDensity f = ∫⁻ a, (f * g) a ∂μ

views.nl_informal:
The Lebesgue integral of `g` with respect to the measure `μ.withDensity f` coincides with
the integral of `f * g`. This version assumes that `g` is almost everywhere measurable. For a
version without conditions on `g` but requiring that `f` is almost everywhere finite, see
`lintegral_withDensity_eq_lintegral_mul_non_measurable`
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.lintegral_withDensity_eq_lintegral_mul₀' {μ : Measure α} {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : AEMeasurable f μ) {g : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hg : AEMeasurable g (μ.withDensity f)) : ∫⁻ a, g a ∂μ.withDensity f = ∫⁻ a, (f * g) a ∂μ

views.nl_informal:
If `f` is almost everywhere positive, then `μ ≪ μ.withDensity f`. See also
`withDensity_absolutelyContinuous` for the reverse direction, which always holds.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.withDensity_absolutelyContinuous' {μ : Measure α} {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : AEMeasurable f μ) (hf_ne_zero : ∀ᵐ x ∂μ, f x ≠ 0) : μ ≪ μ.withDensity f

views.nl_informal: If `μ ≪ ν` and `ν` is s-finite, then `μ` is s-finite.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.sFinite_of_absolutelyContinuous {ν : Measure α} [SFinite ν] (hμν : μ ≪ ν) : SFinite μ

views.nl_informal:
Let `C` be the supremum of `ν s` over all measurable sets `s` such that `μ.restrict s` is
sigma-finite. `C` is finite since `ν` is a finite measure. Then there exists a measurable set `t`
with `μ.restrict t` sigma-finite such that `ν t ≥ C - 1/n`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.exists_isSigmaFiniteSet_measure_ge (μ ν : Measure α) [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (n : ℕ) : ∃ t, MeasurableSet t ∧ SigmaFinite (μ.restrict t) ∧ (⨆ (s) (_ : MeasurableSet s) (_ : SigmaFinite (μ.restrict s)), ν s) - 1/n ≤ ν t

views.nl_informal:
`μ.sigmaFiniteSetWRT' ν` has maximal `ν`-measure among all measurable sets `s` with sigma-finite
`μ.restrict s`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.measure_sigmaFiniteSetWRT' (μ ν : Measure α) [IsFiniteMeasure ν] : ν (μ.sigmaFiniteSetWRT' ν) = ⨆ (s) (_ : MeasurableSet s) (_ : SigmaFinite (μ.restrict s)), ν s

views.nl_informal: For all sets `s` in `(μ.sigmaFiniteSetWRT ν)ᶜ`, if `ν s ≠ 0` then `μ s = ∞`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.measure_eq_top_of_subset_compl_sigmaFiniteSetWRT' [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (hs_subset : s ⊆ (μ.sigmaFiniteSetWRT' ν)ᶜ) (hνs : ν s ≠ 0) : μ s = ∞

views.nl_informal: For all sets `s` in `(μ.sigmaFiniteSetWRT ν)ᶜ`, if `ν s ≠ 0` then `μ s = ∞`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.measure_eq_top_of_subset_compl_sigmaFiniteSetWRT [SFinite ν] (hs_subset : s ⊆ (μ.sigmaFiniteSetWRT ν)ᶜ) (hνs : ν s ≠ 0) : μ s = ∞

views.nl_informal: The measure `μ.restrict μ.sigmaFiniteSetᶜ` takes only two values: 0 and ∞ .
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.restrict_compl_sigmaFiniteSet_eq_zero_or_top (μ : Measure α) [SFinite μ] (s : Set α) : μ.restrict μ.sigmaFiniteSetᶜ s = 0 ∨ μ.restrict μ.sigmaFiniteSetᶜ s = ∞

views.nl_informal: An s-finite measure `μ` is sigma-finite iff `μ μ.sigmaFiniteSetᶜ = 0`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.measure_compl_sigmaFiniteSet_eq_zero_iff_sigmaFinite (μ : Measure α) : μ μ.sigmaFiniteSetᶜ = 0 ↔ SigmaFinite μ

views.nl_informal: **Hahn decomposition theorem**
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.hahn_decomposition (μ ν : Measure α) [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [IsFiniteMeasure ν] : ∃ s, MeasurableSet s ∧ (∀ t, MeasurableSet t → t ⊆ s → ν t ≤ μ t) ∧ ∀ t, MeasurableSet t → t ⊆ sᶜ → μ t ≤ ν t

views.nl_informal:
For a convex continuous function `f` on `[0, ∞)`, if `μ` is absolutely continuous
with respect to a probability measure `ν`, then
`f μ.real univ ≤ ∫ x, f (μ.rnDeriv ν x).toReal ∂ν`.

views.nl_informal:
For a convex continuous function `f` on `[0, ∞)`, if `μ` is absolutely continuous
with respect to `ν`, then
`ν.real univ * f (μ.real univ / ν.real univ) ≤ ∫ x, f (μ.rnDeriv ν x).toReal ∂ν`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.mul_le_integral_rnDeriv_of_ac [IsFiniteMeasure μ] [IsFiniteMeasure ν] (hf_cvx : ConvexOn ℝ (Ici 0) f) (hf_cont : ContinuousWithinAt f (Ici 0) 0) (hf_int : Integrable (fun x ↦ f (μ.rnDeriv ν x).toReal) ν) (hμν : μ ≪ ν) : ν.real univ * f (μ.real univ / ν.real univ) ≤ ∫ x, f (μ.rnDeriv ν x).toReal ∂ν

views.nl_informal:
The Radon-Nikodym derivative of a sigma-finite measure `μ` with respect to another
measure `ν` is `ν`-almost everywhere finite.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.rnDeriv_lt_top (μ ν : Measure α) [SigmaFinite μ] : ∀ᵐ x ∂ν, μ.rnDeriv ν x < ∞

views.nl_informal:
Given measures `μ` and `ν`, if `s` is a measure mutually singular to `ν` and `f` is a
measurable function such that `μ = s + fν`, then `s = μ.singularPart μ`.

This theorem provides the uniqueness of the `singularPart` in the Lebesgue decomposition theorem,
while `MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_rnDeriv` provides the uniqueness of the
`rnDeriv`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart {s : Measure α} {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable f) (hs : s ⟂ₘ ν) (hadd : μ = s + ν.withDensity f) : s = μ.singularPart ν

views.nl_informal:
If a set `s` separates the absolutely continuous part of `μ` with respect to `ν`
from the singular part, then the singular part equals the restriction of `μ` to `s`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.singularPart_eq_restrict' {s : Set α} [μ.HaveLebesgueDecomposition ν] (hμs : μ.singularPart ν sᶜ = 0) (hνs : ν.withDensity (μ.rnDeriv ν) s = 0) : μ.singularPart ν = μ.restrict s

views.nl_informal:
If a set `s` separates `ν` from the singular part of `μ` with respect to `ν`,
then the singular part equals the restriction of `μ` to `s`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.singularPart_eq_restrict {s : Set α} [μ.HaveLebesgueDecomposition ν] (hμs : μ.singularPart ν sᶜ = 0) (hνs : ν s = 0) : μ.singularPart ν = μ.restrict s

views.nl_informal:
Given measures `μ` and `ν`, if `s` is a measure mutually singular to `ν` and `f` is a
measurable function such that `μ = s + fν`, then `f = μ.rnDeriv ν`.

This theorem provides the uniqueness of the `rnDeriv` in the Lebesgue decomposition
theorem, while `MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart` provides the uniqueness of the
`singularPart`. Here, the uniqueness is given in terms of the measures, while the uniqueness in
terms of the functions is given in `eq_rnDeriv`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_withDensity_rnDeriv {s : Measure α} {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable f) (hs : s ⟂ₘ ν) (hadd : μ = s + ν.withDensity f) : ν.withDensity f = ν.withDensity (μ.rnDeriv ν)

views.nl_informal:
Given measures `μ` and `ν`, if `s` is a measure mutually singular to `ν` and `f` is a
measurable function such that `μ = s + fν`, then `f = μ.rnDeriv ν`.

This theorem provides the uniqueness of the `rnDeriv` in the Lebesgue decomposition
theorem, while `MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_singularPart` provides the uniqueness of the
`singularPart`. Here, the uniqueness is given in terms of the functions, while the uniqueness in
terms of the functions is given in `eq_withDensity_rnDeriv`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.eq_rnDeriv [SigmaFinite ν] {s : Measure α} {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable f) (hs : s ⟂ₘ ν) (hadd : μ = s + ν.withDensity f) : f =ᵐ[ν] μ.rnDeriv ν

views.nl_informal: The Radon-Nikodym derivative of `f ν` with respect to `ν` is `f`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.rnDeriv_withDensity₀ (ν : Measure α) [SigmaFinite ν] {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : AEMeasurable f ν) : (ν.withDensity f).rnDeriv ν =ᵐ[ν] f

views.nl_informal: The Radon-Nikodym derivative of `f ν` with respect to `ν` is `f`.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.rnDeriv_withDensity (ν : Measure α) [SigmaFinite ν] {f : α → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable f) : (ν.withDensity f).rnDeriv ν =ᵐ[ν] f

views.nl_informal:
The Radon-Nikodym derivative of the restriction of a measure to a measurable set is the
indicator function of this set.
views.lean_signature: theorem MeasureTheory.Measure.rnDeriv_restrict_self (ν : Measure α) [SigmaFinite ν] {s : Set α} (hs : MeasurableSet s) : (ν.restrict s).rnDeriv ν =ᵐ[ν] s.indicator 1

views.nl_informal:
Radon-Nikodym derivative of the scalar multiple of a measure.
See also `rnDeriv_smul_left'`, which requires sigma-finite `ν` and `μ`.

views.nl_informal:

sets, for any measurable set `E` of finite positive measure, the set `E / E` is a neighbourhood of

views.nl_informal:
**Uniqueness of left-invariant measures**: In a second-countable locally compact group, any
σ-finite left-invariant measure is a scalar multiple of the Haar measure.
This is slightly weaker than assuming that `μ` is a Haar measure (in particular we don't require
`μ ≠ 0`).

for a statement not assuming second-countability.

views.nl_informal:
Let `μ` be a σ-finite left invariant measure on `G`. Then `μ` is equal to the Haar measure
defined by `K₀` iff `μ K₀ = 1`.

views.nl_informal:

on some compact set with non-empty interior.

views.nl_informal:
The image of an additive Haar measure under a surjective linear map is proportional to a given
additive Haar measure. The proportionality factor will be infinite if the linear map has a
nontrivial kernel.

views.nl_informal:

additive Haar measure, with a positive (but maybe infinite) factor.

views.nl_informal:
Given a surjective linear map `L`, it is equivalent to require a property almost everywhere
in the source or the target spaces of `L`, with respect to additive Haar measures there.

views.nl_informal:
Given a linear map `L : E → F`, a property holds almost everywhere in `F` if and only if,
almost everywhere in `F`, it holds almost everywhere along the subspace spanned by the
image of `L`. This is an instance of a disintegration argument for additive Haar measures.

views.nl_informal:

suffices to check it almost everywhere along all translates of a given vector subspace. This is an
instance of a disintegration argument for additive Haar measures.

views.nl_informal:
The volume form coming from an orientation in an inner product space gives measure `1` to the
parallelepiped associated to any orthonormal basis. This is a rephrasing of

views.nl_informal:
In an oriented inner product space, the measure coming from the canonical volume form
associated to an orientation coincides with the volume.
views.lean_signature: theorem Orientation.measure_eq_volume (o : Orientation ℝ F (Fin n)) : o.volumeForm.measure = volume

views.nl_informal:

of the restriction, `μ_𝓕`, of a right-invariant measure `μ` to a fundamental domain `𝓕`, is the

This is the **Unfolding Trick**: Given an additive subgroup `Γ'` of an additive group `G'`, the
integral of a function `f` on `G'` times the lift to `G'` of a function `g` on the quotient
`G' ⧸ Γ'` with respect to a right-invariant measure `μ` on `G'`, is equal to the integral over
the quotient of the automorphization of `f` times `g`.

then a.e. all points belong to finitely sets of the family.

E.g., if `α` is an (e)metric space and `m u = ∞` on any set of diameter `≥ r`, then this lemma
implies that `μ (s ∪ t) = μ s + μ t` on any two sets such that `r ≤ edist x y` for all `x ∈ s`
and `y ∈ t`.

views.nl_informal:

The value of the Infimum of a nonempty family of outer measures on a set is not simply

**The Hahn decomposition theorem**: Given a signed measure `s`, there exist

**The Jordan decomposition theorem**: Given a signed measure `s`, there exists a pair of
mutually singular measures `μ` and `ν` such that `s = μ - ν`. In this case, the measures `μ`
and `ν` are given by `s.toJordanDecomposition.posPart` and
`s.toJordanDecomposition.negPart` respectively.

signed measure corresponding to
`s.toJordanDecomposition.posPart - s.toJordanDecomposition.negPart`.

views.nl_informal:
**The Lebesgue Decomposition theorem between a signed measure and a measure**:
Given a signed measure `s` and a σ-finite measure `μ`, there exist a signed measure `t` and a
measurable and integrable function `f`, such that `t` is mutually singular with respect to `μ`
and `s = t + μ.withDensityᵥ f`. In this case `t = s.singularPart μ` and
`f = s.rnDeriv μ`.

mutually singular with respect to `μ` and `s = t + μ.withDensityᵥ f`, we have
`t = singularPart s μ`, i.e. `t` is the singular part of the Lebesgue decomposition between
`s` and `μ`.

views.nl_informal:
Given a measure `μ`, signed measures `s` and `t`, and a function `f` such that `t` is
mutually singular with respect to `μ` and `s = t + μ.withDensityᵥ f`, we have
`f = rnDeriv s μ`, i.e. `f` is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of `s` and `μ`.

views.nl_informal:
A countably generated structure is ultrahomogeneous if and only if any equivalence between
finitely generated substructures can be extended to any element in the domain.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.isUltrahomogeneous_iff_IsExtensionPair (M_CG : CG L M) : L.IsUltrahomogeneous M ↔ L.IsExtensionPair M M

views.nl_informal: If a class has a Fraïssé limit, it must be Fraïssé.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.IsFraisseLimit.isFraisse [Countable (Σ l, L.Functions l)] [Countable M] (h : IsFraisseLimit K M) : IsFraisse K

views.nl_informal: The Fraïssé limit of a class is unique, in that any two Fraïssé limits are isomorphic.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.IsFraisseLimit.nonempty_equiv : Nonempty (M ≃[L] N)

views.nl_informal:
Any countable infinite structure in the empty language is a Fraïssé limit of the class of finite
structures.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.empty.isFraisseLimit_of_countable_infinite (M : Type*) [Countable M] [Infinite M] [Language.empty.Structure M] : IsFraisseLimit { S : Bundled Language.empty.Structure | Finite S } M

views.nl_informal: The class of finite structures in the empty language is Fraïssé.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.empty.isFraisse_finite : IsFraisse { S : Bundled.{w} Language.empty.Structure | Finite S }

views.nl_informal:
Any countable nonempty model of the theory of dense linear orders is a Fraïssé limit of the
class of finite models of the theory of linear orders.

views.nl_informal: The class of finite models of the theory of linear orders is Fraïssé.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.isFraisse_finite_linear_order : IsFraisse {M : CategoryTheory.Bundled.{0} Language.order.Structure | Finite M ∧ M ⊨ Language.order.linearOrderTheory}

views.nl_informal: The theory of dense linear orders is `ℵ₀`-categorical.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.aleph0_categorical_dlo : (ℵ₀).Categorical Language.order.dlo

views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.dlo_isComplete : Language.order.dlo.IsComplete

views.nl_informal:
An alternate characterization of an extension pair is that every finitely generated partial
isomorphism can be extended to include any particular element of the domain.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.isExtensionPair_iff_exists_embedding_closure_singleton_sup : L.IsExtensionPair M N ↔ ∀ (S : L.Substructure M) (_ : S.FG) (f : S ↪[L] N) (m : M), ∃ g : (closure L {m} ⊔ S : L.Substructure M) ↪[L] N, f = g.comp (Substructure.inclusion le_sup_right)

views.nl_informal:
For a countably generated structure `M` and a structure `N`, if any partial equivalence
between finitely generated substructures can be extended to any element in the domain,
then there exists an embedding of `M` in `N`.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.embedding_from_cg (M_cg : Structure.CG L M) (g : L.FGEquiv M N) (H : L.IsExtensionPair M N) : ∃ f : M ↪[L] N, g ≤ f.toPartialEquiv

views.nl_informal:
For two countably generated structure `M` and `N`, if any PartialEquiv
between finitely generated substructures can be extended to any element in the domain and to
any element in the codomain, then there exists an equivalence between `M` and `N`.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.equiv_between_cg (M_cg : Structure.CG L M) (N_cg : Structure.CG L N) (g : L.FGEquiv M N) (ext_dom : L.IsExtensionPair M N) (ext_cod : L.IsExtensionPair N M) : ∃ f : M ≃[L] N, g ≤ f.toEmbedding.toPartialEquiv

views.nl_informal:
The **Compactness Theorem of first-order logic**: A theory is satisfiable if and only if it is
finitely satisfiable.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.Theory.isSatisfiable_iff_isFinitelySatisfiable {T : L.Theory} : T.IsSatisfiable ↔ T.IsFinitelySatisfiable

views.nl_informal: Any theory with an infinite model has arbitrarily large models.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.Theory.exists_large_model_of_infinite_model (T : L.Theory) (κ : Cardinal.{w}) (M : Type w') [L.Structure M] [M ⊨ T] [Infinite M] : ∃ N : ModelType.{_, _, max u v w} T, Cardinal.lift.{max u v w} κ ≤ #N

views.nl_informal:
A version of The Downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem where the structure `N` elementarily embeds
into `M`, but is not by type a substructure of `M`, and thus can be chosen to belong to the universe
of the cardinal `κ`.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementaryEmbedding_card_eq_of_le (M : Type w') [L.Structure M] [Nonempty M] (κ : Cardinal.{w}) (h1 : ℵ₀ ≤ κ) (h2 : lift.{w} L.card ≤ Cardinal.lift.{max u v} κ) (h3 : lift.{w'} κ ≤ Cardinal.lift.{w} #M) : ∃ N : Bundled L.Structure, Nonempty (N ↪ₑ[L] M) ∧ #N = κ

views.nl_informal:
The **Upward Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem**: If `κ` is a cardinal greater than the cardinalities of
`L` and an infinite `L`-structure `M`, then `M` has an elementary extension of cardinality `κ`.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementaryEmbedding_card_eq_of_ge (M : Type w') [L.Structure M] [iM : Infinite M] (κ : Cardinal.{w}) (h1 : Cardinal.lift.{w} L.card ≤ Cardinal.lift.{max u v} κ) (h2 : Cardinal.lift.{w} #M ≤ Cardinal.lift.{w'} κ) : ∃ N : Bundled L.Structure, Nonempty (M ↪ₑ[L] N) ∧ #N = κ

views.nl_informal:
The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem: If `κ` is a cardinal greater than the cardinalities of `L`
and an infinite `L`-structure `M`, then there is an elementary embedding in the appropriate
direction between then `M` and a structure of cardinality `κ`.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementaryEmbedding_card_eq (M : Type w') [L.Structure M] [iM : Infinite M] (κ : Cardinal.{w}) (h1 : ℵ₀ ≤ κ) (h2 : lift.{w} L.card ≤ Cardinal.lift.{max u v} κ) : ∃ N : Bundled L.Structure, (Nonempty (N ↪ₑ[L] M) ∨ Nonempty (M ↪ₑ[L] N)) ∧ #N = κ

views.nl_informal:
A consequence of the Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem: If `κ` is a cardinal greater than the
cardinalities of `L` and an infinite `L`-structure `M`, then there is a structure of cardinality `κ`
elementarily equivalent to `M`.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.exists_elementarilyEquivalent_card_eq (M : Type w') [L.Structure M] [Infinite M] (κ : Cardinal.{w}) (h1 : ℵ₀ ≤ κ) (h2 : lift.{w} L.card ≤ Cardinal.lift.{max u v} κ) : ∃ N : CategoryTheory.Bundled L.Structure, (M ≅[L] N) ∧ #N = κ

views.nl_informal:
An alternative statement of the Compactness Theorem. A formula `φ` is modeled by a
theory iff there is a finite subset `T0` of the theory such that `φ` is modeled by `T0`
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.Theory.models_iff_finset_models {φ : L.Sentence} : T ⊨ᵇ φ ↔ ∃ T0 : Finset L.Sentence, (T0 : L.Theory) ⊆ T ∧ (T0 : L.Theory) ⊨ᵇ φ

views.nl_informal: The Łoś–Vaught Test : a criterion for categorical theories to be complete.

views.nl_informal:
The **Downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem** :
If `s` is a set in an `L`-structure `M` and `κ` an infinite cardinal such that
`max (#s, L.card) ≤ κ` and `κ ≤ # M`, then `M` has an elementary substructure containing `s` of
cardinality `κ`.

views.nl_informal: Two substructures are equal if they have the same elements.
views.lean_signature: theorem FirstOrder.Language.Substructure.ext {S T : L.Substructure M} (h : ∀ x, x ∈ S ↔ x ∈ T) : S = T

views.nl_informal: The substructure generated by a set includes the set.

views.nl_informal: A substructure `S` includes `closure L s` if and only if it includes `s`.

views.nl_informal:
Substructure closure of a set is monotone in its argument: if `s ⊆ t`,
then `closure L s ≤ closure L t`.

views.nl_informal:
An induction principle for closure membership. If `p` holds for all elements of `s`, and

If `s` is a dense set in a structure `M`, `Substructure.closure L s = ⊤`, then in order to prove

Möbius inversion for functions to a `CommGroup`, where the equalities only hold on a

views.nl_informal: Odd Bernoulli numbers (greater than 1) are zero.
views.lean_signature: theorem bernoulli'_odd_eq_zero {n : ℕ} (h_odd : Odd n) (hlt : 1 < n) : bernoulli' n = 0

views.nl_informal:
**Faulhaber's theorem** relating the **sum of p-th powers** to the Bernoulli numbers:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k^p = \sum_{i=0}^p B_i\binom{p+1}{i}\frac{n^{p+1-i}}{p+1}.$$
See https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Faulhaber%27s_Formula and [orosi2018faulhaber] for
the proof provided here.
views.lean_signature: theorem sum_range_pow (n p : ℕ) : (∑ k ∈ range n, (k : ℚ) ^ p) = ∑ i ∈ range (p + 1), bernoulli i * ((p + 1).choose i) * (n : ℚ) ^ (p + 1 - i) / (p + 1)

views.nl_informal:
Alternate form of **Faulhaber's theorem**, relating the sum of p-th powers to the Bernoulli
numbers: $$\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^p = \sum_{i=0}^p (-1)^iB_i\binom{p+1}{i}\frac{n^{p+1-i}}{p+1}.$$
Deduced from `sum_range_pow`.
views.lean_signature: theorem sum_Ico_pow (n p : ℕ) : (∑ k ∈ Ico 1 (n + 1), (k : ℚ) ^ p) = ∑ i ∈ range (p + 1), bernoulli' i * (p + 1).choose i * (n : ℚ) ^ (p + 1 - i) / (p + 1)

views.lean_signature: theorem Polynomial.bernoulli_generating_function (t : A) : (mk fun n => aeval t ((1 / n ! : ℚ) • bernoulli n)) * (exp A - 1) = PowerSeries.X * rescale t (exp A)

views.nl_informal: The inequality which contradicts Bertrand's postulate, for large enough `n`.
views.lean_signature: theorem bertrand_main_inequality {n : ℕ} (n_large : 512 ≤ n) : n * (2 * n) ^ sqrt (2 * n) * 4 ^ (2 * n / 3) ≤ 4 ^ n

views.nl_informal:
A lemma that tells us that, in the case where Bertrand's postulate does not hold, the prime
factorization of the central binomial coefficient only has factors at most `2 * n / 3 + 1`.
views.lean_signature: theorem centralBinom_factorization_small (n : ℕ) (n_large : 2 < n) (no_prime : ¬∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ n < p ∧ p ≤ 2 * n) : centralBinom n = ∏ p ∈ Finset.range (2 * n / 3 + 1), p ^ (centralBinom n).factorization p

views.nl_informal:
An upper bound on the central binomial coefficient used in the proof of Bertrand's postulate.
The bound splits the prime factors of `centralBinom n` into those
1. At most `sqrt (2 * n)`, which contribute at most `2 * n` for each such prime.
2. Between `sqrt (2 * n)` and `2 * n / 3`, which contribute at most `4^(2 * n / 3)` in total.
3. Between `2 * n / 3` and `n`, which do not exist.
4. Between `n` and `2 * n`, which would not exist in the case where Bertrand's postulate is false.
5. Above `2 * n`, which do not exist.
views.lean_signature: theorem centralBinom_le_of_no_bertrand_prime (n : ℕ) (n_large : 2 < n) (no_prime : ¬∃ p : ℕ, Nat.Prime p ∧ n < p ∧ p ≤ 2 * n) : centralBinom n ≤ (2 * n) ^ sqrt (2 * n) * 4 ^ (2 * n / 3)

views.nl_informal: Proves that **Bertrand's postulate** holds for all sufficiently large `n`.

views.nl_informal:

descending list of primes, each no more than twice the next, such that the list contains a witness
for each number ≤ n.

views.nl_informal:
**Bertrand's Postulate**: For any positive natural number, there is a prime which is greater than
it, but no more than twice as large.
views.lean_signature: theorem Nat.exists_prime_lt_and_le_two_mul (n : ℕ) (hn0 : n ≠ 0) : ∃ p, Nat.Prime p ∧ n < p ∧ p ≤ 2 * n

views.nl_informal:
If `a^(p-1) = 1 mod p`, but `a^((p-1)/q) ≠ 1 mod p` for all prime factors `q` of `p-1`, then `p`
is prime. This is true because `a` has order `p-1` in the multiplicative group mod `p`, so this
group must itself have order `p-1`, which only happens when `p` is prime.

and `a^((p-1)/q) ≠ 1 mod p` for all prime factors `q` of `p-1`.
The multiplicative group mod `p` is cyclic, so `a` can be any generator of the group
(which must have order `p-1`).
views.lean_signature: theorem reverse_lucas_primality (p : ℕ) (hP : p.Prime) : ∃ a : ZMod p, a ^ (p - 1) = 1 ∧ ∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → q ∣ p - 1 → a ^ ((p - 1) / q) ≠ 1

views.nl_informal:
